\chapter{Communication Complexity — One Way Minimax}
%%% generated by the blueprint pipeline from TCSlib.CommunicationComplexity.NewmanTheorem.OneWayMinimax
\section{Overview}

This module establishes Yao's minimax principle for one-way public-coin communication
protocols.  It introduces the distributional error of a deterministic one-way protocol
and proves that if every deterministic protocol of cost at most $n$ suffers distributional
error exceeding $\varepsilon$ under some joint input distribution, then the one-way
public-coin communication complexity at error $\varepsilon$ exceeds $n$.

%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%%
\section{Declarations}

\begin{definition}[Distributional error of a one-way protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError}
\statementsource{roughgarden-cc-oneway}{
  pdf-043896d6545f-p012-b003,
  pdf-043896d6545f-p012-b004
}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace}
Given a deterministic one-way protocol $p$ computing a function
$f : X \to Y \to \alpha$, and a finite probability distribution $\mu$ on $X \times Y$,
the \emph{distributional error} of $p$ with respect to $\mu$ and $f$ is the real number
\[
  \Pr_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\bigl[p.\mathrm{run}(x,y) \neq f(x,y)\bigr],
\]
i.e.\ the $\mu$-measure of the set of inputs on which the protocol's output disagrees
with $f$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Deterministic protocol from public-coin protocol]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol}
Given a one-way public-coin protocol $p$ over a randomness space $\Omega$ and a fixed
coin outcome $\omega \in \Omega$, \texttt{toDeterministic}~$p$~$\omega$ is the
deterministic one-way protocol obtained by substituting $\omega$ for the public
randomness: it uses the same message type and sends/decodes by fixing $\omega$ in $p$.
\end{definition}

\begin{theorem}[Fixing the coin recovers the randomised run]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_run}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.run, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a one-way public-coin protocol with shared-randomness type $\Omega$, input
types $X$ and $Y$, and output type $\alpha$; let $\omega \in \Omega$ be a coin outcome
and $x \in X$, $y \in Y$ be inputs. Fixing the public coin at $\omega$ turns $p$ into a
deterministic one-way protocol, and executing that deterministic protocol on inputs $x$
and $y$ yields the same output as running $p$ on the joint inputs $(\omega, x)$ for
Alice and $(\omega, y)$ for Bob. In both cases the output is Bob's decoder applied to
his input $(\omega, y)$ together with the message that Alice's encoder assigns to
$(\omega, x)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Cost invariance under derandomization]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_cost}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_cost}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic}
\difficulty{1}
Let $p$ be a one-way public-coin protocol over a shared randomness type $\Omega$, with
input types $X$, $Y$ and output type $\alpha$, and let $\omega \in \Omega$ be a fixed
coin outcome. Then the deterministic one-way protocol obtained from $p$ by substituting
$\omega$ for the public randomness has the same communication cost as $p$; that is, both
have cost $\lceil \log_2 |M| \rceil$ bits, where $M$ is the shared message codebook.
\end{theorem}

\begin{lemma}[Exchanging the order of integration for the failure probability]
\lean{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.failureIntegral_swap}
\label{CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.failureIntegral_swap}
\leanok
\uses{CommunicationComplexity.CoinTape, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.measureReal_eq_integral_indicator_one, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.rrun}
\difficulty{5}
Let $X \times Y$ be a finite set equipped with a probability measure $\mu$, let $p$ be a
one-way public-coin protocol with inputs in $X$ and $Y$, outputs in $\alpha$, and shared
randomness ranging over coin tapes of length $m$, and let $f : X \times Y \to \alpha$ be
a target function. Write $\mathrm{rrun}(p, x, y, \omega)$ for the output produced by
running $p$ on inputs $x$ and $y$ under coin tape $\omega$, and let $\nu$ be the measure
carried by the coin tapes of length $m$. Then
\[
  \int \mu\bigl(\{(x,y) : \mathrm{rrun}(p,x,y,\omega) \neq f(x,y)\}\bigr)\,d\nu(\omega)
  \;=\;
  \int \nu\bigl(\{\omega : \mathrm{rrun}(p,x,y,\omega) \neq f(x,y)\}\bigr)\,d\mu(x,y),
\]
where each measure is read as a real number. That is, integrating the $\mu$-probability
of failure over the choice of coin tape yields the same value as integrating the
$\nu$-probability of failure over the choice of input pair.
\end{lemma}

\uses{CommunicationComplexity.CoinTape, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.cost, CommunicationComplexity.Deterministic.OneWay.Protocol.distributionalError, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.integral_le_of_le, CommunicationComplexity.FiniteProbabilitySpace.lt_integral_of_lt, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.rrun, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.Protocol.toDeterministic_run, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.communicationComplexity_le_iff, CommunicationComplexity.PublicCoin.OneWay.failureIntegral_swap}
\difficulty{5}
Let $f : X \to Y \to \alpha$ be a function, let $\varepsilon \in \bbr$, and let $n \in
\bbn$. Suppose there is a finite probability distribution $\mu$ on $X \times Y$ under
which every deterministic one-way protocol $p$ of communication cost at most $n$ has
distributional error strictly greater than $\varepsilon$; that is,
$\Pr_{(x,y)\sim\mu}\bigl[\,p\text{ outputs a value}\neq f(x,y)\,\bigr] > \varepsilon$
for every such $p$. Then the $\varepsilon$-error one-way public-coin communication
complexity of $f$ is strictly greater than $n$.
\end{theorem}
